intro: Tamba maps two trees on opposite sides of a large merged municipality. Kinone-bashi, a zelkova whose root arches underground across the Okumura River, stands by an 11th-century shrine in Kashiwara, under treatment for root rot since 2002. The Kyushaku-fuji of Byakugo-ji, one wisteria plant trained along 120 metres of trellis, flowers a taxi ride away in Ichijima each May, both reached from stations on the same rail line.
meta_description: Tamba, Japan: a zelkova whose root bridges a river by an 11th-century shrine, and a wisteria trained 120 metres, both free or near-free to visit.
question_meta: Tamba's oldest mapped tree is Kinone-bashi, a zelkova roughly 1,000 years old; the Kyushaku-fuji wisteria flowers each May a taxi ride away.
question_answer: Tamba's oldest mapped tree is Kinone-bashi, a Saw-leaf Zelkova estimated at roughly 1,000 years old, beside Kashiwara Hachiman Shrine. The Kyushaku-fuji of Byakugo-ji, a single wisteria vine trained along a 120-metre trellis, stands in Ichijima, on the other side of Tamba City; nobody has recorded when it was planted.
question_context:
A root did what no engineer asked it to do: one of Kinone-bashi's roots grew thick enough to span the Okumura River underground, arching about ten metres beneath a riverbed roughly six metres wide. It stands beside the approach to Kashiwara Hachiman Shrine, founded in 1024, at 6.4 metres round, the largest zelkova in Tamba City. Hyogo Prefecture designated it a Natural Monument in 1970, and the city has treated a root-rot fungus there since 2002. It is a short walk from JR Kashiwara Station.

The Kyushaku-fuji is a different kind of tree: one wisteria root trained along 120 metres of trellis at Byakugo-ji temple in the Ichijima hills. Kyushaku-fuji, nine-shaku wisteria, is a cultivar name rather than a measurement; the longest recorded flower chain is 180cm. Early May brings a festival with the trellis lit after dark. The last five kilometres from Ichijima Station are an eight-minute taxi ride; entry is 300 yen. The two trees sit 7.5km apart, both on the JR Fukuchiyama Line but different stops.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Tamba?
faq.a: Kinone-bashi, a Saw-leaf Zelkova estimated at roughly 1,000 years old, standing beside the approach to Kashiwara Hachiman Shrine.

faq.q: What does the name Kinone-bashi mean?
faq.a: Tree-root bridge. One of the zelkova's roots grew thick enough to span the Okumura River underground, arching about ten metres beneath the riverbed.

A single wisteria vine, cultivar Noda Naga-fuji, trained along 120 metres of trellis at Byakugo-ji temple in Ichijima, on the other side of Tamba City from Kinone-bashi. It flowers in late April and early May.
Kinone-bashi is free. Byakugo-ji charges 300 yen entry and is reached by an eight-minute taxi from Ichijima Station; no bus or safe walking route exists.
Kinone-bashi is not currently healthy: a root-rot fungus, Armillaria tabescens, has been treated by the city since 2002. No health concerns are recorded for the Kyushaku-fuji.

trees.story:
A root did what no engineer asked it to do. One of this zelkova's roots grew thick enough to span the Okumura River underground, arching about ten metres beneath a riverbed roughly six metres wide, so that the ground on either bank is connected by living wood rather than a bridge. The name follows the shape: Kinone-bashi, the tree-root bridge.

The tree stands beside the approach to Kashiwara Hachiman Shrine, founded in 1024, in the Hyogo town of Kashiwara. At 6.4 metres round and about 21 metres tall, with a crown spreading some 25 metres in every direction, it is the largest zelkova in Tamba City. Hyogo Prefecture designated it a Natural Monument in March 1970.

It is not currently a healthy tree, and the story should say so rather than look away from it. Armillaria tabescens, a root-rot fungus, entered through damage left by past road and bridge construction nearby, and the city has been treating the infection since 2002, cutting out decayed wood and applying antagonistic fungi to slow it. The tree is roughly 1,000 years old by local estimate, though nobody has cored it.

It stands a short walk from JR Kashiwara Station on the Fukuchiyama Line, free and open, the root bridge visible from the path.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the single root arching underground across the Okumura River like a bridge. It stands beside the approach to Kashiwara Hachiman Shrine.

trees.name: The Kyushaku-fuji of Byakugo-ji

location.address: 709 Byakugoji, Ichijima-cho, Tamba City, Hyogo Prefecture 669-4334

trees.access: Paid entry, 300 yen per person. Temple grounds open 9:00-17:00 (until 21:00 during the wisteria's night illumination period in late April/early May). Best reached by taxi (about 8 minutes) from JR Fukuchiyama Line's Ichijima Station; no bus route or safe walking distance from the station, and the temple runs no shuttle.
trees.transport: JR Fukuchiyama Line, Ichijima Station, then approx. 8 minutes by taxi (about 5km). By car, 10 minutes from the Kasuga IC on the Maizuru-Wakasa Expressway.
trees.story:
The longest flower chain recorded on this wisteria measured 180 centimetres. The name promises more. Kyushaku-fuji reads as nine-shaku wisteria, about 2.7 metres, and the temple's own head priest has gone on record correcting visitors who take it as a measurement: it is the cultivar name, Noda Naga-fuji, a plant bred for unusually long racemes.

One plant, one root, trained along 120 metres of trellis in the grounds of Byakugo-ji, a Tendai temple in the hills of Tamba founded by tradition in 705. That date belongs to the temple and says nothing about the vine. Nothing else does either: no source checked, the temple's own site included, gives a planting date, an age or a trunk measurement. If you know when it went in, tell us.

What is documented is the flowering. Early May brings the Kyushaku-fuji festival, and through late April and early May the trellis is lit after dark, with the grounds staying open until nine instead of five. Entry is 300 yen.

Getting there is the awkward part. The last five kilometres from Ichijima station are a taxi ride of about eight minutes: no bus runs it, the temple operates no shuttle, and the road is not one to walk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trellis it covers, one vine trained along 120 metres of frame, with flower chains up to 180 centimetres in early May. It is the only structure of that length in the grounds of Byakugo-ji.

best_time.label: late April into early May, when the racemes hang and the trellis is lit after dark
